title: Jesse Collet & Keni - Fireside chat about the development of NetHack
speaker: Jesse Collet & Keni
talk_title: Fireside chat about the development of NetHack
description: Host Alexei Pepers and Jesse Collet and Keni (former NetHack devs) talk about the early days of NetHack and the role of open-source development in Roguelike games.

segments.text: >> Morning. ALEXEI: I tried to pitch
having a hooded figure visual effect to lean into the secrecy but it is great to just, you know,
have you here to chat. I will say for people in the discussion since this is an AMA I will be
keeping an eye on questions as we talk, so, please submit those. Don't just wait until the end. This
is a discussion. Let's kicko ff by introductions and maybe a bit of what was your history as a
member of the NetHack dev team and things you contributed to. We can start with you, Keni.
KENI: OK. I got into NetHack through Rogue. And then in graduate school,
I was porting everything I could to the omega because I had a bunch of friends I had forced
to buy them instead of Apples and needed to prove to them that this computer could
handle all this stuff. So I hit NetHack in comp sources games. It didn't work. This was
my first experience with what I guess would be called a meme these days of NetHack breaks
compilers. I also broke the compiler on the Cray. -- with NetHack. Many people
have done it with other things. But through the discussion with dev team about that bug,
I ended up on the Amiga porting team and did that for years and years and then as the Amiga
was petering out the web was coming in so I moved over to the building of our website and then more
email tools and back-end stuff. Occasionally I dipped my toe in the main part of the game.
ALEXEI: Excellent. Jesse, how about you? JESSE: I skipped Rogue. I think I started
directly with Hack if I remember correctly. I was very young. I discovered computer games on
Unix systems either at companies I worked for or at universities. At the time, computers were kind
of a rarity. So we didn't have access to that much games. And like Keni the first thing I did was to
port it on some system that didn't support it. At that time I put NetHack 3.2 came out which was a
direct descendent of Hack and I really got into it and started porting it to wherever I needed
to port and one thing led to another and I fixed bugs and you have to remember that at the time,
the community was working in a very different way. We had Use Net with built-in boards. Whatever you
posted, you fixed the bugs and you posted the difs. Here is the fix for that particular bug
or that kind of thing. Once you do that, after that you start having your own ideas on how to
improve the game and you start posting suggestions with the code because you tested it. And I did a
number of patches like that and that's why I got contacted by the -- at the time dev team
in 1988 so, you know, within the first year of the creation of NetHack and I joined the team to start
working on NetHack 3.0 which was a very first version with a really full dev team at the time.
I stayed active for quite a long time. Let's see. About 12-13 years. And around the turn
of the century, I kind of went off but I still stayed connected to the team. I am
still technically part of the dev team and get the emails wherever anyone sends suggestions
but I haven't contributed in 20 years except maybe some discussions and stuff like that.
ALEXEI: That's wonderful. I think the format of the dev team is both kind of familiar to
like some people are doing open source and have GIT repos and how did that work in terms
of deciding which directions to take NetHack in? Was it a lot of discussions within the dev team?
Are there certain people that own that and over time is it a lot of people coming and
going and passing the torch of like now you are going to start taking charge of this element?
JESSE: That's a great question. KENI: Yeah.
JESSE: It is also one that is very hard to actually answer because I suppose it depends a lot
on that time period that you are looking at. But for the time I was on the team, there was no real
leadership so to speak. Nobody was deciding what the others would do and so on. We were discussing
ideas over email basically and usually societies would come up in the form of here is what I coded,
what do you think about it? And then usually, it would evolve from there. What I realize much
later on in my life is that it was actually very close to what the improv mechanisms are which is
now that I look back we never said no or but. We also said yes and you try to improve on what
was done. That's why I always insist on saying that, you know, NetHack is first and foremost a
collaborative project. Nobody owned any part of the code. Nobody own any part of the features.
Everybody worked on everything basically. When I say everybody, there is a dev team, but we got
so many contributions from all of the players that it is very hard to keep track of that.
KENI: From my point of view, I guess the timeframe is just a little different. I came
in when Ischock Mailer was the librarian. He is not a programmer. He was in charge of the source
tree which at that point in time was sitting on some computer at the University of Pennsylvania
and if you needed a new copy, he would make a copy and mail it to you as a large tar ball.
Other than that it was up to you to keep up with your email and apply patches and then
they started failing you got to start again. JESSE: Yeah, no [indiscernible] at the time.
ALEXEI: Of course. JESSE: It is true. Hit shack was very much
the moderator of the team in many ways. He was, if I remember correctly, a professor in philosophy,
so that gives you an idea of his background. He was a great guy. I miss him terribly to be fair.
KENI: Yes. JESSE: He was much more the
stabilizing core of the team than somebody who would tell you what to do and what not to do.
KENI: I keep waiting to find out he has left a book, you know? Peering at us as lab rats.
Let's see what happens if we try to develop a game using this organizational format.
ALEXEI: Yeah, it is beautiful. I think in librarian is a beautiful term for that. I
think it is amazing, a lot of projects have failed due to lack of structure and things
like that. For it to stay so collaborative, and I think that's very beautiful too. When
I first got in touch with you, Jesse, you told me about how I think the roguelike
community jokes about the NetHack dev team being secretive and you are like,
no, it is more about embracing the fact it is not just a select set of people who built
NetHack and it is this community effort and I think that's a lovely way to think of it.
JESSE: I can tell you when you send that mail initially asking if you wanted to speak
anonymously it got a good laugh from the team. KENI: Yeah, I think it is more obviously
collaborative now but it has always been attached pretty sturdily to at least those
people who are willing to reach out to us. ALEXEI: Right. Yeah. Yeah. No, that's wonderful.
JESSE: To give you an example, recently NetHack got added to the collection of the museum of
modern New York and when the creator asked us, you know, who should we attribute it,
without any discretion we knew it would have to be the NetHack dev team period.
Nobody else. That's really important to us. ALEXEI: Yeah. I think that that is wonderful.
That's why I am glad to get to do this because so many people have been inspired about NetHack
and want to know more about the history and the development. A lot of people in
this community have done scraping of -- I know people who would kill to read those emails of
the yes/and development of NetHack over time. JESSE: We should have kept them, yes. It wasn't
a law to keep that stuff at the time. ALEXEI: Absolutely. I will grab a question
from the audience from jines. It is about the fact there are so many community projects that
build off NetHack and forks and I don't know if you have heard of Facebook is
created this environment to train AI agents on playing NetHack because their argument was
that NetHack is this super rich game that's not very resource intensive so it is something that,
you know, they can work with that just has so much complexity. How does it feel? Have you heard
things like that? How do you feel about these even huge companies are using NetHack as this perfect
example of this really unique game? JESSE: [Laughter] Go ahead,
Keni. I am lost there. KENI: I hadn't heard that. People
shouldn't feel afraid to contact us and, you know, if you have some piece of news like that,
we will add it to the web page. I actually went to the MOMA opening with my wife and we have been
married 25 years but I think getting into MOMA and being there and seeing other developers of
much more visually exciting games, like NetHack, oh, wow. That's so important in my life. It just
gave her a better perspective -- I am not just wasting my time completely. And honestly, it was
good for me too because I don't think we get the feedback that we could because we spend all our
time writing it and not so much sitting around in chat rooms listening to people talk about it.
JESSE: Yeah, actually, I realize something leading up to that talk is that I was reminiscing and what
struck me is NetHack didn't become kind of famous until very late in its lifetime. Until I would
say the late '90s, you know? We only heard from the community for direct -- from the mid to late
'90s we started getting queries from journalists who wanted to write articles, authors who wanted
to write books and so on and that was kind of wow. How did that happen? Are you sure they are talking
about NetHack? Not confusing it with something else? I think to me the day it really dawned on
me is when we received male from the Blizzard North -- mail -- who sent an email saying when
they pitched Diablo to their management they said we want to do NetHack with graphics and
sounds. That they had been inspired by that. And I looked at it and I had played Diablo like crazy at
the time so I looked at that mail and my mind was blown. It is another one of those emails I wish I
had kept. Sometimes you are stupid, you know? ALEXEI: I am glad to have this event because it
is. NetHack is so beloved and a huge influence. It is still like coming up constantly. Actually,
this is a question we had yesterday a talk from Kes about the asphynx and the prominence of the
encyclopedia and digging back to the asphynx. Did either of you ever contribute to things
like the encyclopedia and did people throw in let's have a reference to this and that or
were some people really more into that? KENI: Well, I actually dug through the commits,
and a lot of what I did happened before we got to GIT or even subversion. So exactly what line,
you know, is mine, long gone. Some of my jokes are in there. I never did anything like a monster. It
is just not the way I tend to approach things. I am responsible for the ripped screen on the Amiga
that has a moving moon. It is really terrible because I am not an artist but I think that was
the first not completely ASCII art rip screen. ALEXEI: Wow. Amazing.
KENI: Just little things that have gotten lost. I think I did fake mail. I couldn't
prove it from the history we've got. ALEXEI: Can you explain fake mail briefly?
KENI: Once upon a time if you run NetHack on a system you are sharing with 500 friends,
when you get mail, email in our mailbox, it will show up as a scroll in NetHack.
JESSE: You would have the mail demon show up actually.
KENI: Yes. And when I moved NetHack to the Amiga, I missed that. It was the occasional interruption
that was kind of fun so, I believe it was me, I just added this thing that just triggered the mail
demon relatively randomly and a bunch of pieces of mail that obviously aren't real because you
can't extract the mail from a PC real well. ALEXEI: That's wonderful. I am pretty sure,
and someone can correct me if I am wrong, I think if you play NetHack
in the browser and I believe there is a way to send messages to people who are
playing NetHack in the browser and look in the game and it uses the mail demon system
to deliver that message. That's repurposed. JESSE: I had completely forgotten about the
mail demon. We tried it as a UNIX joke because the mail demon is what distributes emails on UNIX.
KENI: If you don't remember that, nobody is going to remember most of what I do.
ALEXEI: Some of us remember. People at this conference.
KENI: How many people have dug into 3.7 code enough to know I added sandboxing.
Or the crashing port stuff. JESSE: Not very user-facing.
KENI: Actually, the data librarian, the code isn't mine but the original concept was. Not the kind of
user-facing stuff that people really know. ALEXEI: But crucial for it to run. I work in
the source code and I had a talk actually once that was a guide to reading the source
code of NetHack just because there is so many amazing comments and really clever functions.
My favorite was string kitten instead of string cat for concatenating one character. It was
lovely. I was surprised by just how much code is in there for porting and supporting so many
different systems which makes a lot of sense given just like the community nature of it but, yeah,
there is so much work in there. People don't see it other than the fact they see NetHack runs on
their system whatever their system is. JESSE: It was a hit dev nightmare for a
long time. Going through the code because you had code for porting and also certain
features that could be turned on and off. We had let's stop with the nonsense and
made options completely permanent so we wouldn't have to deal with that.
ALEXEI: What character class is your favorite? Either to play
or conceptually? Another audience question. KENI: I honestly play whatever it brings up under
random because I honestly don't play much these days. If I want to do something with NetHack,
I want to change it, add something to it. If I am playing it, it means I am debugging something
specific. If you want stories, how frustrated I get actually playing something like NetHack, I
managed to get my hands on a tandem that was being decommissioned and had privileges on that for a
while. Sorry. It was a pyramid not a tandem. The first thing I did was I built a version of Rogue
with like a plus 50 broad sword and plus 50 armor just so I could see how it went after the first
couple levels. Yeah. I don't actually play much. JESSE: Yeah, I ended up in the same situation
in the later years. I played more and more for debugging and testing purposes
than actually playing itself. If I remember, I used to favor the knight
mostly because I would go after Excalibur. ALEXEI: Same reason. Here is another question. Are
there any other from a nonsense contributions or systems that you are personally proud of no matter
how back end and invisible they might be? JESSE: In my case, I think the biggest thing
I remember starting, because, again, you know, you start something, you don't do it,
was the special levels. Initially, NetHack was just completely procedurally generated and since
we were all trying to tell stories, because a lot of inspiration from NetHack comes from
literature and so on, I wanted to start to add some, you know, pre-designed environments. And
the challenge was multiple because -- the first one was you don't want to lose the
randomness and what makes the game what it is, you know, every place is different. If
you start with levels that are the same it would lower that fun. How can I have a preconceived,
pre-designed environment in a random environment while keeping that path? And that was what we
used to call at the time the reveler compiler and the reason we went with the compiler is we didn't
want to leave too much hints on the file systems because multi-user systems and so on and people
could read the files. Everything was compiled in advance. On top of that, avoiding compiling you
catch errors early instead of during runtime. So I designed the very first level like that which was
the castle at the bottom of the normal dungeon. And later on, the one that I am really proud of
was Vladivostok? I remember reading years and years later that it was the most evil part of
NetHack for a lot of people because -- at the time I wanted to really break the idea that each
level is completely independent from the previous one. So I got the idea of having something that's
spread over three levels or more. It is a fair number that were three. To get to the top level
we had to first enter at the bottom level. So I had to create a -- I had to take into account a
number of things. And, you know, first part was that, OK, how do I stop them from getting to the
top level without going from the bottom so digging holes and teleporting and I had to add a lot of
mechanisms to prevent that stuff. And then we had the stairs problem where at the time it was very
straightforward. You know, you take the stairs down, generate the next level, and you look where
the stairs are and put the player there. Done. Well, once you have two stairs, one outside and
one inside, you have a problem. I went with a hack for lack of a better word and introduced ladders.
You know that way I would connect two ladders and the stairs would connect and that was it.
That triggered a discussion that came up to a few design for the stairs where we could now connect
stairs between levels and that led later on to the branches system and the branches in the dungeon. I
didn't do that but that kind of evolved that way. I got really fond memories of all that work.
ALEXEI: That's wonderful. What about you, Keni? Do you have any other particular
moments you are especially proud of? KENI: Oh, um. I have mentioned most of what's
still there. One thing maybe I will mention for history books is something that never got subtle
light of day. The Amiga port was starting to run out of RAM and so the PC port had an overlay
system, so I went and wrote an overlay system for the Amiga but I didn't like how intrusive
the PC port -- the PC overlay system was. You had everything function needed a declaration about
where it was going and it was a frequent cause of breakage. Unfortunately, the way I did this was to
run the source code through a modified version of GCC that would figure out where everything had to
go and set-up the tables and rewrite the code to do that. Then we went to think about distributing
this and I asked Jim Stalman is this OK? I need to send this one file from GCC and he says no, you
have to send the entire GCC distribution. Since at that point, distributing NetHack was already
something that required a lot of coordination with the moderators for comp sources games because it
was the largest thing that got distributed by I don't know a factor of 5 or 10 depending on the
year. The idea of making it 10 times larger so this one port could have this one file -- so,
yeah. That never happened but it did work. ALEXEI: [Laughter] now everyone knows. I am
glad you got a chance to share. One question I think is fun, you know, one of the most famous
phrases I think associated with NetHack is the dev team thinks of everything. How does that feel
when you are on the dev team? KENI: It is a challenge.
JESSE: No pressure there. KENI: Yeah, every time I see a patch go by,
because internally while we are using GIT, it does get mailed to us so we have a chance to
comment on each individual thing or fork a discussion. Each time I see a patch go by,
it is like OK, but what if you did this in this situation? Sometimes I will send
email about that which people will generally reject. And sometimes I will write a piece of
code. But yeah. I look at it as a challenge. JESSE: Actually, you would be surprised that
initially, you know, we would be very surprised at what the players would attempt and report on.
So a lot of the dev team thinks of everything is kind of taking credit for all those people's
suggestions or even, you know, trying to do something. One of my favorite ones was
the polypiling of the metal. We didn't see that one coming for sure. I will tell you that. That
the player would start piling up worms on top of each other and that one of the polymorphs
to try get more worms. We didn't see that one coming but we said yeah, that's smart
and we tonight -- don't want to stop that. That wouldn't be fair. But we added the possibility of
integrating the objects when zapping around or one of polymorph because then you have a
risk that comes with that plus a limited amount of charges. That's very much what I was saying
about the yes/and. We take all that stuff coming in and say first question is does make sense?
If it makes sense, how can we make it work? ALEXEI: Yeah, no, I think that's beautiful. I
love that that's still a lesson people can take today and that I think, yeah, explains a lot of
how NetHack got to where it is, and it is very neat to see how it is an evolving process and it
got to what it is because of so many people working together in the community and the
developers. Thank you. We are at time. I will say I want to just Thank you in terms of I got started
at Roguelike Celebration talking about NetHack and got into roguelikes because of NetHack and my
mother wanted to thank you because she plays NetHack and that's how I got into it. She told
me I probably wouldn't exist without NetHack because she started dating my father because he
had a computer and if she started dating him she would be able to play NetHack on his computer. I
wouldn't be here without NetHack in many ways. KENI: It is not my story to tell but that is not
the only marriage associated with NetHack. ALEXEI: My fiancé went to the MOMA NetHack
together. Thank you so much for being here. This is really special. Thanks so much for taking the
time. I am glad to get the chance to be kind of a voice for the community that is so thankful for
all of the work you did on this wonderful game. KENI: Thank you.
JESSE: Well, Thank you. It was great to be here. Always just love to talk about NetHack.
It has been a huge part of my life. I can't shut up about it when you get me started.
